name: Internet access
plain: Lets the app use the network; granted automatically on Android.
meaning: Lets an app send any data off the device. The permission is auto-granted so the real controls are network policies and user data toggles.

android.revocation: Settings > Apps > Mobile data and Wi-Fi (OEM) can restrict
android.store_policy: Play: none; cleartext blocked by default for apps targeting 9+
android.note: Android 9 (API 28) blocks cleartext HTTP by default (usesCleartextTraffic false).

ios.prompt_ui: Cellular data toggle only; no prompt
ios.store_policy: App Review 2.5; ATS requires HTTPS since 2017
ios.note: iOS apps have network access by default; ATS enforces HTTPS.

limits.headline: Can use the internet, which Android grants at install and iPhone allows by default
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens whenever the app loads or sends something
can: Send and receive data over Wi-Fi or cellular
Load pages, sync accounts and upload files
cannot: Use unsecured HTTP by default on Android 9 and newer
Use unsecured HTTP on iPhone without an App Transport Security exception
Be switched off by a permission prompt; you can use Airplane mode or block cellular data in Settings
limits.differs: Android lists the permission at install with no prompt. iPhone gives network access by default and enforces HTTPS.

story.what_it_is: The basic right to use the internet, which Android gives every app without asking.
story.for_you: You never see a prompt for it. Almost every app can send and get data from the internet the moment you install it. The real choices for you are in settings, like turning off cellular data for one app.
story.for_makers: Makers need it for nearly everything: ads, sync, updates and analytics. Because it is auto granted, there is no friction. It is also how any app can send data off your phone.

use_cases.example: A game connects to its server for matches, chat and anti cheat.
A social app loads your feed and sends your posts.
A streaming app downloads video and sends watch history.
A free app loads ads and sends back data about which ones you saw.
A bank app sends transfers over an encrypted link.
A crash tool uploads error reports to a developer's server.

story.android_note: Android grants it to every app at install and offers data and background toggles in settings.
story.ios_note: iPhone has no network permission, though you can turn off cellular data for each app.

technical_bounds: Cellular and Wi-Fi data restrictions are user choices

history.change: Cleartext traffic disabled by default for apps targeting 9
App Transport Security required for App Store apps from Jan 2017
